title: Jan 2019 (Abu Dhabi)
des: DOH (HAAD) paediatrics recall, Abu Dhabi exam January 2019. Answers checked and explained.

questions.question: A sexually active adolescent girl has had regular periods since puberty but no period for 8 weeks. She has no hirsutism and her breasts are mature. What is the most appropriate next test?
questions.exp: Pregnancy is the most common cause of secondary amenorrhoea in an adolescent who is sexually active, so a pregnancy test always comes first, before any other investigation. Then consider prolactin, TFTs, FSH/LH and androgens.

questions.question: An obese adolescent girl (BMI 36) has had irregular periods since puberty and hirsutism on the face and upper arms. There is a family history of type 2 diabetes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: PCOS: oligomenorrhoea plus clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism (hirsutism, acne), often with obesity, insulin resistance (acanthosis nigricans) and a family history of type 2 diabetes. In adolescents, both irregular cycles (persisting beyond 2 years after menarche) and hyperandrogenism are needed. Rapid virilisation suggests a tumour; check 17-OHP for non-classical CAH.

questions.question: In the same girl with suspected polycystic ovary syndrome, which test best supports the diagnosis?
questions.exp: In adolescents, PCOS is diagnosed by irregular periods plus hyperandrogenism, ideally shown biochemically (raised total or free testosterone). Pelvic ultrasound is NOT recommended for diagnosis within 8 years of menarche, because multifollicular ovaries are normal at this age; it is used only to exclude other causes such as tumours. Also check TFTs, prolactin and 17-OHP to exclude mimics.

questions.question: What is the appropriate management for this obese adolescent with polycystic ovary syndrome?
questions.a: Lifestyle changes with diet and exercise, plus a combined oral contraceptive pill for the periods and hirsutism
questions.b: Metformin alone, with no lifestyle advice
questions.e: No treatment until she wants to become pregnant
questions.exp: Weight loss through diet and exercise is first-line in every overweight girl with PCOS: even 5–10% loss improves cycles and androgens. The combined oral contraceptive pill regulates periods, protects the endometrium and reduces hirsutism and acne. Metformin is added for insulin resistance or impaired glucose tolerance; anti-androgens (spironolactone) are added after 6 months of COCP if hirsutism persists, and need contraception.

questions.question: A sexually active adolescent girl has a purulent vaginal discharge and a red, inflamed vulva. She has had unprotected sex. What is the most likely cause?
questions.exp: A purulent (pus-like) discharge after unprotected sex suggests gonorrhoea (often with chlamydia, so test and treat both). Candida gives a thick white curd-like discharge with itching; bacterial vaginosis (Gardnerella) gives a thin grey fishy discharge without inflammation; HSV gives painful ulcers. Test with NAAT, treat with ceftriaxone, treat partners and screen for other STIs.

questions.question: Which test confirms the diagnosis of autoimmune haemolytic anaemia?
questions.exp: The direct antiglobulin test detects antibody (IgG) or complement (C3) already bound to the patient's red cells, which defines autoimmune haemolysis. The indirect Coombs test looks for free antibodies in serum (used in antenatal and cross-match testing). Osmotic fragility/EMA binding is for hereditary spherocytosis.

questions.question: A child has acute haemolysis with low haemoglobin and high reticulocytes. The direct Coombs test is positive for IgG, and the antibody reacts at body temperature (37°C). What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Warm AIHA: IgG antibodies that bind best at 37°C, causing extravascular haemolysis in the spleen, with spherocytes. Treat with steroids. Cold agglutinin disease is IgM (after Mycoplasma or EBV), active below 37°C, and fixes complement (C3 positive). Paroxysmal cold haemoglobinuria (Donath–Landsteiner IgG antibody) follows viral infections in children.

questions.question: A child with sickle cell disease gets parvovirus B19 infection (fifth disease). What is he at risk of?
questions.exp: Parvovirus B19 infects red cell precursors and stops red cell production for 7–10 days. With the short red cell lifespan in sickle cell disease, Hb falls fast with a very low reticulocyte count (transient aplastic crisis). Treat with blood transfusion; recovery comes with returning reticulocytes. Isolate from pregnant staff and other patients with haemolytic anaemia.

questions.question: A newborn baby has petechiae. He is otherwise well and feeding normally, and the blood count shows thrombocytopenia. What is the most appropriate first step towards diagnosis?
questions.d: Take the maternal history and check the mother's platelet count
questions.exp: In a well neonate with thrombocytopenia, the cause is usually immune. A low maternal platelet count (or a history of ITP or lupus) points to maternal autoimmune thrombocytopenia; a normal maternal count points to neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia. A sick baby needs a sepsis screen.

questions.question: A child has recurrent prolonged fevers. Full blood count shows a white cell count of 6,000 with only 0.4% neutrophils. What is the most appropriate first step?
questions.b: Oral antibiotics and review in a week
questions.d: Wait for blood culture results before treating
questions.e: Bone marrow biopsy before any treatment
questions.exp: The absolute neutrophil count is 6,000 x 0.004 = 24/microL: severe neutropenia. Fever with severe neutropenia is a medical emergency: take blood cultures and start IV broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour. Then investigate the cause (repeated counts for cyclic neutropenia, bone marrow, antineutrophil antibodies).

questions.question: A child is pale. Blood count shows low haemoglobin, low MCV and a high RDW. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Iron deficiency gives a microcytic anaemia with a HIGH RDW (red cells of different sizes) and a low ferritin. Thalassaemia trait gives a microcytosis that is out of proportion to the mild anaemia, a normal RDW, a high red cell count and a Mentzer index (MCV/RBC) under 13.

questions.question: A child has an abdominal mass, and examination shows hemihypertrophy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Hemihypertrophy (Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome, or isolated) raises the risk of embryonal tumours, especially Wilms tumour and hepatoblastoma. A smooth flank mass that does not cross the midline in a well child is typical of Wilms. Children with hemihypertrophy need abdominal ultrasound every 3 months until 7–8 years (and AFP for hepatoblastoma in BWS).

questions.question: In disseminated intravascular coagulation, how do fibrin degradation products (FDPs) make bleeding worse?
questions.e: They block fibrin polymerisation and platelet aggregation (an anticoagulant effect)
questions.exp: In DIC, widespread clotting uses up platelets and clotting factors, and fibrinolysis produces FDPs and D-dimers. FDPs interfere with fibrin monomer polymerisation and platelet function, adding to the bleeding. Treat the cause, and give platelets, FFP and cryoprecipitate (fibrinogen) if bleeding.

questions.question: Which result confirms beta-thalassaemia trait?
questions.exp: Beta-thalassaemia trait: mild microcytic anaemia with a normal ferritin and a raised HbA2 (3.5–7%) on electrophoresis or HPLC. Iron deficiency can lower HbA2, so correct iron first. HbH inclusions are seen in alpha-thalassaemia (HbH disease).

questions.question: A child has autoimmune haemolytic anaemia and immune thrombocytopenia together. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Evans syndrome is autoimmune destruction of two or more blood cell lines (Coombs-positive haemolytic anaemia with ITP, sometimes neutropenia). It is chronic and relapsing, and can be linked to immune dysregulation (ALPS, CVID) or lupus. Treat with steroids, IVIG and second-line immunosuppression.

questions.question: A child has acute haemolysis with a fast heart rate after a viral illness. A mass (the spleen) is felt in the left hypochondrium, the blood film shows spherocytes and the direct Coombs test is positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Spherocytes are seen in both hereditary spherocytosis and AIHA; the positive direct Coombs test makes this AIHA. Children with sickle cell disease lose their spleen function early (autosplenectomy), and G6PD deficiency shows bite and blister cells with a negative Coombs test.

questions.question: A child with sickle cell disease comes to the emergency department with right upper quadrant pain. What is the most likely cause?
questions.exp: Chronic haemolysis produces bilirubin (pigment) gallstones in up to 50% of children with sickle cell disease by adolescence, causing biliary colic and cholecystitis. Do an ultrasound; elective cholecystectomy is advised for symptomatic stones. Hepatic sequestration and sickle hepatopathy are rarer causes of RUQ pain, with a rapidly enlarging liver and falling Hb.

questions.question: A child has acute haemolysis after taking a sulfonamide drug. What is the definitive diagnostic test?
questions.exp: Oxidant drugs (sulfonamides, primaquine, nitrofurantoin), fava beans and infections trigger haemolysis in G6PD deficiency. The blood film shows bite and blister cells and Heinz bodies. Confirm with a quantitative G6PD assay; during an acute episode young red cells have more enzyme, giving a falsely normal result, so repeat it 2–3 months later if normal.

questions.question: A 3-year-old boy develops acute haemolysis with low Hb and high reticulocytes after eating fava beans. The direct Coombs test is negative. What is the most likely cause?
questions.exp: Coombs-negative acute haemolysis after fava beans (favism) is G6PD deficiency, an X-linked disorder common in the Middle East. Haemolysis is intravascular (dark urine), with bite cells. Avoid triggers; transfuse if severe. A positive Coombs test would point to an immune cause.

questions.question: A child has progressive tiredness. Blood tests show a high white cell count, anaemia and thrombocytopenia, and there is generalised lymphadenopathy. What is the most diagnostic test?
questions.exp: Leukaemia (most often ALL) is suggested by two or more cell lines being abnormal, lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly. A blood film may show blasts, but bone marrow aspiration (with immunophenotyping and cytogenetics) confirms and classifies it (more than 20–25% blasts). Get a chest X-ray before anaesthesia to look for a mediastinal mass.

questions.question: After a bout of gastroenteritis, a child has puffy eyelids and reduced urine. Tests show haemolysis (low Hb, high reticulocytes), thrombocytopenia and high urea and creatinine. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Typical HUS follows bloody diarrhoea from Shiga-toxin E. coli (O157:H7): microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (fragmented red cells, Coombs negative), thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury. Coagulation is usually normal (unlike DIC). Management is supportive (fluids, dialysis if needed); antibiotics and antimotility drugs should be avoided in STEC diarrhoea.

questions.question: A mother brings her son to the emergency department because his sibling died suddenly. What is the most appropriate next test for this child?
questions.e: A 12-lead ECG, with a full history and examination
questions.exp: Sudden cardiac death in a young relative may be due to an inherited condition: long QT, Brugada, catecholaminergic VT, WPW or cardiomyopathy. Screen siblings with a careful history (syncope, palpitations, family history) and examination, then a 12-lead ECG, plus echocardiography and exercise testing, and genetic testing if a cause is found.

questions.question: A child has tachycardia, tachypnoea, a gallop rhythm and an enlarged tender liver. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
questions.exp: These are signs of congestive heart failure (fluid overload with hepatic congestion). First give a diuretic, oxygen and treatment of the cause. A fluid bolus would make it worse. Beta-blockers are started later for chronic heart failure, not in acute decompensation.

questions.question: An infant has tachycardia and tachypnoea. Three days ago he had fever and a runny nose. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Myocarditis often follows a viral illness (coxsackie B, adenovirus, parvovirus B19): unexplained tachycardia out of proportion to fever, tachypnoea, gallop rhythm, hepatomegaly and heart failure or shock. ECG shows low voltages and ST changes, troponin is raised, and the echo shows a poorly contracting, dilated left ventricle. Rheumatic fever is rare under 5 years.

questions.question: An infant has a heart rate of 260/min with a narrow QRS, pallor and no murmur. The rest of the examination is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: In infants, SVT is usually above 220/min, with a fixed rate, no beat-to-beat variation and absent or abnormal P waves. Sinus tachycardia is usually under 220/min and varies. Treat a stable child with vagal manoeuvres (ice to the face), then IV adenosine; synchronised cardioversion if shocked.

questions.question: A well child who is growing normally has a grade 2/6 systolic murmur at the upper left sternal border with an ejection click. The murmur does not change with position. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: An innocent murmur changes with position (softer when sitting or standing) and has no click. A murmur that does not change with posture, with an ejection click that varies with breathing, suggests pulmonary valve stenosis. Confirm with echocardiography; mild stenosis needs only follow-up, while moderate to severe stenosis is treated by balloon valvuloplasty.

questions.question: A child has supravalvular aortic stenosis with narrowing of the coronary artery origins. Which syndrome is most likely?
questions.exp: Williams syndrome (7q11.23 deletion including the elastin gene): elfin face, friendly "cocktail party" personality, intellectual disability, hypercalcaemia, and an elastin arteriopathy causing supravalvular aortic stenosis, peripheral pulmonary stenosis, coronary ostial stenosis and renal artery stenosis. Noonan has pulmonary stenosis; Turner has bicuspid aortic valve and coarctation.

questions.question: A child has had fever for 6 days with a rash, bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, a strawberry tongue and peeling of the fingers and toes. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Fever for 5 days or more with conjunctivitis, oral changes, rash, extremity changes and cervical lymphadenopathy is Kawasaki disease. Peeling of the fingertips starts in the second to third week. Scarlet fever has exudative tonsillitis and a sandpaper rash, toxic shock has hypotension, and measles has cough, coryza and Koplik spots.

questions.question: What is the treatment of choice for this child with Kawasaki disease?
questions.exp: IVIG 2 g/kg as one infusion, plus aspirin, ideally within the first 10 days, prevents most coronary aneurysms. Do an echocardiogram at diagnosis and at 2 and 6 weeks. Live vaccines are delayed for 11 months after IVIG.

questions.question: Which statement about lumbosacral myelomeningocele is correct?
questions.a: Hydrocephalus occurs in fewer than 10% of cases
questions.b: Bladder and bowel function are always normal
questions.c: No child with myelomeningocele can ever walk, even with support
questions.d: Most children develop hydrocephalus, and around 80% need a shunt
questions.exp: Myelomeningocele is usually linked to the Chiari II malformation, and 80–90% develop hydrocephalus (many need a VP shunt). Walking depends on the level: most children with low lumbar or sacral lesions walk, often with orthoses. Neurogenic bladder and bowel are almost universal. Most have normal or near-normal intelligence. Prevention: folic acid 400 micrograms before conception (5 mg if high risk).

questions.question: A child on an antiepileptic drug develops pancreatitis and raised liver enzymes. Which drug is most likely to be responsible?
questions.exp: Sodium valproate can cause pancreatitis (check amylase if abdominal pain and vomiting) and hepatotoxicity, which can be fatal, especially under 2 years, with polytherapy, or with mitochondrial disease (POLG, Alpers). Other side effects: weight gain, tremor, hair loss, thrombocytopenia, hyperammonaemia and teratogenicity.
